prompt: How verbose should identifier names be?
helper: A loop index inside a 5-line function vs. a variable that lives across a 200-line module.
prose: I prefer short, terse identifiers. Loop indices are `i`, contexts are `ctx`, requests are `req`. Names get longer only when scope demands it.
I lean terse. Short names for short-lived locals, longer names for cross-module things. Don't bloat names just to be self-documenting.
I match name length to scope: terse for short-lived locals, descriptive for anything that crosses function or module boundaries.
I lean descriptive. I'd rather see `requestContext` than `ctx` in most places, but a 3-line loop can still use `i`.
I want fully descriptive names everywhere. `iteratorIndex` over `i`, `requestContext` over `ctx`. Names should read like prose.
glance: Names lean terse for locals; longer for cross-boundary things.
Names are fully descriptive, no single-letter or abbreviated identifiers.

prompt: How do you case acronyms inside identifiers?

choices.label: parseURL, fetchHTTP
choices.prose: Acronyms stay fully uppercase inside identifiers: `parseURL`, `fetchHTTP`, `userID`.

choices.label: parseUrl, fetchHttp
choices.description: Acronyms are treated like normal words.
choices.prose: Acronyms are title-cased like normal words: `parseUrl`, `fetchHttp`, `userId`.
choices.avoids: Don't leave acronyms all-caps inside camelCase identifiers.

choices.label: It depends
choices.description: Long acronyms title-case; short ones (ID, OK) stay uppercase.
choices.prose: Acronym casing depends on length: short ones like `ID`, `OK`, `IO` stay uppercase; longer ones like `HTTP`, `JSON` get title-cased to `Http`, `Json`.

prompt: How do you name boolean variables?

choices.label: `isReady`, `hasItems`, `canEdit`
choices.prose: Booleans use `is`/`has`/`can`/`should` prefixes: `isReady`, `hasItems`, `canEdit`, `shouldRetry`.

choices.label: `ready`, `dirty`, `editable`
choices.prose: Booleans use adjective-style names without prefixes: `ready`, `dirty`, `editable`, `pending`.
choices.glance: Booleans are bare adjectives, no `is`/`has` prefix.

choices.label: Whichever reads more naturally in context
choices.prose: Boolean names follow whichever reads more naturally. `dirty` is fine on its own; `isAuthenticated` makes sense when there's no shorter alternative.

prompt: When do you reach for a comment?

choices.label: Only when the *why* is non-obvious
choices.description: Code explains what; comments explain why.
choices.prose: Comments explain *why*, not *what*. Add one only when the reason isn't obvious from the code, a workaround, a non-obvious constraint, a subtle invariant.
choices.glance: Comment only when the **why** is non-obvious.
choices.avoids: Don't add comments that restate what the code already says.

choices.label: Docstrings on public APIs, sparingly inline
choices.description: Top-of-function explanations, otherwise let the code speak.
choices.prose: Public APIs get docstrings (purpose, params, return). Inline comments are reserved for the truly surprising. Internal helpers usually don't need either.
choices.glance: Docstrings on public APIs; sparing inline comments.

choices.label: Liberally, future-me will thank present-me
choices.description: Section headers, intent, non-obvious choices, all documented.
choices.prose: Comment liberally. Section headers, intent at the top of non-trivial functions, notes on why a particular approach was chosen, all useful for future readers.
choices.glance: Comment liberally, section headers, intent, rationale.

choices.label: Almost never, well-named code is the comment
choices.prose: Comments are rare. Good names and clear structure should make the code self-explanatory. If a comment seems needed, that's usually a signal to refactor instead.
choices.glance: Comments almost never, refactor for clarity instead.
choices.avoids: Don't add comments, improve the code instead.

prompt: How dense are comments in code you write?
prose: My code is nearly comment-free, maybe one comment per hundred lines or so.
Comments are sparse, one or two per file, mostly on the trickiest spots.
Comment density is moderate, most non-trivial functions have one or two comments.
I comment fairly densely, most functions have at least one explanatory comment.
My code is heavily commented, multiple comments per function, often with section headers.

prompt: Are TODO/FIXME comments OK in committed code?

choices.label: Yes, if they reference a ticket (TODO(#1234): …)
choices.prose: TODO/FIXME comments are fine but must reference an issue: `TODO(#1234): …`.
choices.avoids: Don't leave untracked TODOs, link them to an issue.

choices.label: Yes, freeform, track it in your head
choices.prose: Freeform TODO/FIXME comments are fine without any tracking link.

choices.label: No, either fix it now or open a real ticket
choices.prose: No TODO/FIXME comments in committed code. Either fix it now or open a real issue and link it from the PR.
choices.glance: No TODO/FIXME comments in committed code.
choices.avoids: Don't leave TODO or FIXME comments, fix or file an issue.

helper: Length you reach for *first* before extracting.
prose: Functions stay small, 15 lines or fewer. I extract aggressively the moment a function grows.
I prefer small functions, typically under 25 lines. Slightly bigger is fine if the body is cohesive.
Function size is moderate, usually 20-40 lines. I extract when a function does more than one thing, not based on line count.
Functions can run longer, 40-60 lines is fine when the work belongs together.
Long functions are fine when the work is cohesive. I'd rather have a clear 80-line function than five tiny helpers no one will recognize.
glance: Functions can run 40-60 lines when cohesive.
Long functions are fine when cohesive, don't shred for size.

choices.label: Guard clauses + early returns
choices.description: Bail out fast, keep the happy path flat.
choices.prose: Early returns and guard clauses keep the happy path flat. Bail out fast on invalid input or special cases.
choices.glance: Use guard clauses + early returns; keep the happy path flat.
choices.avoids: Don't nest the happy path inside `else` branches.

choices.label: One return at the bottom
choices.description: Easier to reason about and to refactor.
choices.prose: Functions have a single return at the bottom. Easier to reason about cleanup and to add tracing.
choices.avoids: Don't scatter returns through guard clauses.

choices.label: Mixed, whichever reads better per function
choices.prose: Mix early returns and single-exit based on what reads better for the specific function. Validation guards at the top, then a clear linear flow.

prompt: When do you extract a helper function?

choices.label: On the second occurrence (rule of two)
choices.prose: Extract a helper on the second occurrence. Two copies is already one too many.

choices.label: On the third occurrence (rule of three)
choices.prose: Wait for the third occurrence before extracting. Two similar lines beats a premature abstraction.
choices.glance: Wait for the rule of three before extracting helpers.
choices.avoids: Don't extract a helper on the second occurrence, wait for the third.

choices.label: When it improves readability, regardless of reuse
choices.prose: Extract whenever it improves readability, even for a one-off. A well-named helper is worth more than reuse.
choices.glance: Extract for readability, not just reuse.

choices.label: Only when it will be reused outside the file
choices.prose: Only extract when the helper will be reused outside its file. Otherwise inline it where it lives.
choices.avoids: Don't extract single-use helpers unless they'll be reused across files.

prompt: How much nesting is too much?
prose: Hard ceiling at two levels of nesting. Beyond that I extract or flatten with early returns.
I cap at two or three levels. Three is the usual signal to refactor.
Three levels is usually fine; four is the signal to flatten or extract.
Four levels is acceptable if the logic genuinely needs it.
Deep nesting is fine when the structure mirrors the problem.
glance: Deep nesting is fine when problem-driven.

choices.label: Throw exceptions
choices.description: Caller catches at the right layer. Standard for the language.
choices.prose: Surface failures by throwing exceptions. Let them propagate; catch at the layer that knows what to do.
choices.avoids: Don't introduce Result/Either types into code that throws.

choices.label: Return a Result/Either type
choices.description: Errors are values; failure is part of the type signature.
choices.prose: Errors are values. Functions that can fail return a Result/Either type so failure shows up in the type signature.
choices.glance: Errors are values, return Result/Either, don't throw.
choices.avoids: Don't throw exceptions for expected failures.

choices.label: Return `[error, value]` tuples
choices.description: Go-style. Check before using the value.
choices.prose: Functions that can fail return `[error, value]` tuples (Go-style). Caller checks the error before using the value.
choices.glance: Return `[error, value]` tuples; check before using the value.

choices.label: Throw at boundaries, return values internally
choices.prose: Throw at module/system boundaries; return error values for internal flow. Boundary code converts between the two.

prompt: Do you define custom error classes/types?

choices.label: Yes, one per failure mode worth distinguishing
choices.prose: Each distinguishable failure mode gets its own error type. Callers can pattern-match without parsing message strings.
choices.glance: Define custom error types per failure mode.

choices.label: A few, domain errors get types, generic ones use built-ins
choices.prose: Domain-specific errors get their own types. Generic failures (I/O, network) use built-in error types with descriptive messages.

choices.label: Rarely, built-in error types + a message field is usually enough
choices.prose: Built-in error types with descriptive messages are usually enough. Custom error classes are over-engineering for most failures.
choices.avoids: Don't introduce custom error classes unless callers need to distinguish them.

prompt: How granular should try/catch blocks be?
leftLabel: Tight, wrap the single failing call
prose: Try/catch blocks wrap the single line that can fail. Anything more is over-broad.
Try/catch blocks stay tight, wrap the smallest section that can throw.
Try/catch granularity is moderate: wrap the logical unit that can fail, not just one line.
Try/catch tends to wrap larger sections to keep the happy path uncluttered.
Try/catch usually wraps the whole function or major block. Centralize error handling.

prompt: Catching and ignoring an error, ever OK?

choices.label: Never, at minimum, log it
choices.prose: Never swallow errors silently. At minimum, log them with context.
choices.glance: Never swallow errors silently, at minimum, log them.

choices.label: Only with a comment explaining why
choices.prose: Errors can be swallowed, but only with a comment explaining why ignoring this specific error is safe.
choices.avoids: Don't swallow errors without a comment explaining why.

choices.label: Sometimes, cleanup paths, best-effort retries
choices.prose: Some errors can be ignored, cleanup paths that already failed, best-effort retries, optional features. Use judgment.
